It is a fire sensitive obligate seeder, common in the understorey in heath and woodlands along the east coast and ranges of New South Wales, Australia (Weston 2002).; [primary juvenile period: abstract, pdf p. 1] The primary juvenile period of plants was 7-8 years, within the period of likely return fire intervals in the study area.; [age at first flowering from seed: text, pdf p. 5] No plants flowered until 6 years after the fire.; [sample size: methods, pdf p. 3] New seedlings (71) were identified by their distinctive cotyledons.; [site, rainfall, fire type and season: methods, pdf p. 2] We examined a population of *P. lanceolata* at one site within Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park 20 km north of Sydney (33°53' E, 151°13' S) southeastern Australia. ... The site was burnt by an extensive summer (January) wildfire in 1994 that burnt all the surrounding habitat.

data_quote: [fire response: text, p. 39] While the fire killed many of the existing *Senecio* plants some survived by resprouting from a rootstock.; [fire response: text, p. 42] This study indicates that *S. garlandii* is principally a seeder although some plants function as sprouters after a low-intensity fire.; [age at first flowering from seed: text, p. 40] In mid-December 1992, 44% of the 143 remaining *Senecio* plants were flowering or had finished flowering and in late January 1993 flowering had finished. ... In December 1993 more than 95% of the 122 plants surviving their third summer had flowered or were flowering.; [site: text, p. 36] At only 340 ha, The Rock Nature Reserve (lat. 35° 16' S, long. 147° 05' E) is a small island of remnant native vegetation, surrounded by extensive agricultural lands.; [fire season: text, p. 36] After less than 75 mm of rain during November 1990 to March 1991 (average 208 mm for this period) the first major fire (15–17 March 1991) in 40 years burnt more than 90% of The Rock Nature Reserve (personal observation).; [post-fire rainfall: text, p. 43] This suggests that a low fire intensity, combined with more than the about 25 mm of rainfall received in the 2.5 months after the March fire (Fig. 2), then more *Senecio* rootstocks may have resprouted.
notes: fire_response_categorical_surv1: fire killed many plants and some resprouted from a rootstock (p. 39), principally a seeder although some plants function as sprouters (p. 42), less than 5% of the original population remained in leaf (p. 35), read as mostly killed, some resprout; resprouter_type: paper also says a specialised rootstock or similar organ does not appear to be present (p. 43); age_at_first_flower_production_from_seed_repr3: no seedlings flowered in their first year, 44% of the 143 surviving seedlings flowered in their second year (mid-december 1992) and over 95% of 122 plants in their third year, 'second year' read as 2 years (p. 40); sample_size is the 143 surviving seedlings; resprouted rootstocks had flower primordia by mid-october 1991 and had finished flowering by late november 1991, no duration given (p. 39; p. 40); rainfall_post_fire_mm printed as 'about 25 mm' in the 2.5 months after the march fire (p. 43); rainfall before the fire was less than 75 mm from november 1990 to march 1991, average 208 mm (p. 36); fire_season_categorical derived from fire dates 15-17 march 1991; fire origin and severity not stated
source: burrows, g. e. (1995). post-fire regeneration and growth of senecio garlandii (asteraceae) — a vulnerable plant of the south western slopes, nsw. cunninghamia, 4(1), 35-44.

data_quote: [fire response: results, pdf p. 4] The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4).; [time to first flowering of resprouts: results, pdf p. 4] The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks.; [sites: methods, pdf p. 3] At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.).; [fire type and season: methods, pdf p. 2] The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest.
